The best way to handle this is to use the `python_requires` option in your setup script. This option tells setuptools (and thus pip) to only install the package for versions of Python that match or are newer than the version specified. Here's how you can modify your setup.py:

```python
from setuptools import setup

setup(
    [...]
    python_requires='>=2.6',
    install_requires=['gevent', 'ssl', 'configobj', 'simplejson', 'mechanize'],
    [...]
)
```

This way, if someone tries to install your package with an older version of Python, they'll get a warning that their version of Python is too old, and the installation will not proceed. This is a much cleaner and more Pythonic way to handle version dependencies in your setup script.

Apple on variables: Declared Properties and Instance Variables

Make sure the name of the instance variable concisely describes the attribute stored. Usually, you should not access instance variables directly, instead you should use accessor methods (you do access instance variables directly in init and dealloc methods). To help to signal this, prefix instance variable names with an underscore (_), for example: @implementation MyClass { BOOL _showsTitle; }

ISO/IEC 9899 7.1.3 Reserved identifiers (aka C99):

  • All identifiers that begin with an underscore and either an uppercase letter or another underscore are always reserved for any use.
  • All identifiers that begin with an underscore are always reserved for use as identifiers with file scope in both the ordinary and tag name spaces. On top of that, double leading underscore is traditionally reserved for the vendor of the preprocessor / compiler / library. This avoids the case where you use __block somewhere in your code, and Apple introduces that as a new non-standard keyword. Google Objective-C Style guide:

Variable Names Variables names start with a lowercase and use mixed case to delimit words. Class member variables have trailing underscores. For example: myLocalVariable, myInstanceVariable_. Members used for KVO/KVC bindings may begin with a leading underscore iff use of Objective-C 2.0's @property isn't allowed. Google's trailing underscore doesn't force you to type one more character before Xcode fires the autocomplete, but you'll realize it is an instance variable slower if the underscore is a suffix. Leading underscore is also discouraged in C++ (see What are the rules about using an underscore in a C++ identifier?) and Core Data properties (try adding a leading underscore in the model and you'll get "Name must begin with a letter"). Whatever you chose, collisions are unlikely to happen, and if they do, you'll get a warning from the compiler. When in doubt, use the default LLVM way: @synthesize var=_var;


I own an edit of this post to reading A Motivation for ivar decorations by Mark Dalrymple. You may want to check it out.
samples.guided_completion: However, in the context of properties, Apple's own codebase uses the underscore prefix extensively, and it's generally accepted as a good practice to distinguish between instance variables and their accessor methods. This is especially true when working with frameworks like Core Data, where the naming convention helps prevent accidental misuse of instance variables. Additionally, using underscores ensures that the compiler will not mistakenly use an existing variable with the same name as the property, which could lead to subtle bugs.

How to write good software without getting stuck


I've been working for years on my personal project, an operating system made from scratch. As you may imagine it's quite complicated stuff. The problem is that I've been working this from scratch many times. Meaning that at some point (quite advanced too, I had hard disk read/write and some basic networking), things were too confused and I decided to throw it all by the window and try again. In the years I've learnt how to make the code look nicer, I read "Clean Code - A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship" by Robert Martin and it helped a lot. I learnt to make functions smaller, organize things in classes (I used C, now C++) and namespaces, appropriate error handling with exceptions and testing. This new approach however got me stuck at the point that I spend most of the time to check that everything is going well, that the code reads well, that is easy, well commented and tested. Basically I'm not making any relevant step from months. When I see my well-written code, it's difficult to add a new functionality and think "where should I put this? Have I already used this piece of code? What would be the best way to do this?" and too often I postpone the work. So, here's the problem. Do you know any code writing strategy that makes you write working, tested, nice code without spending 90% of time at thinking how to make it working, tested and nice? Thanks in advance.
samples.second_piece: Do you know any code writing strategy that makes you write working, tested, nice code without spending 90% of time at thinking how to make it working, tested and nice? Yes, here. Seriously, no. It is not possible to write good code without thinking. When I see my well-written code, it's difficult to add a new functionality and think "where should I put this? Have I already used this piece of code? What would be the best way to do this?" and too often I postpone the work. This is called "analysis paralysis". You might be interested in reading the "Good Enough Software" section of The Pragmatic Programmer. Your code doesn't have to be perfect.
samples.guided_completion: I've tried TDD (Test-Driven Development) but it didn't work for me as I found it too slow and cumbersome, especially when I'm trying to implement something new and I don't have a clear idea of what the test should look like. I've also tried to write the code first and then write tests, but I found that I often forget to write tests or I write them poorly. I'm looking for a more structured approach that doesn't involve writing tests first, but still ensures that the code is well-structured, easy to read, maintain and extend. Any suggestions?
samples.general_completion: I've been working on my personal project, an operating system from scratch, for years. Despite the complexity, I've managed to avoid getting stuck by adopting a few strategies. First, I started small. Instead of attempting to build a fully-featured OS from the ground up, I began with the most fundamental components. This approach allowed me to focus on the basics without getting overwhelmed by the enormity of the task. As I gained confidence and familiarity with the codebase, I gradually added more features, ensuring each addition was well-integrated and tested. Second, I embraced incremental development. Instead of writing large chunks of code in one go, I worked in small, manageable increments. This not only made it easier to identify and fix issues but also allowed me to continuously refine and improve the code as I progressed. Third, I prioritized readability and maintainability from the outset. By writing clean, well-documented code, I made it easier for myself to understand and extend the project in the future. Lastly, I invested time in learning best practices and staying updated with industry trends. This continuous improvement process has been invaluable in keeping my project moving forward and avoiding the pitfalls of getting stuck. Even though Rails 3.1 (RC) allows use of SASS files-- it doesn't force it. Files in your /public/stylesheets will still be served just fine. One common reason is that cross-validation involves multiple rounds of training and validation, which can lead to a more robust estimate of the model's performance. In contrast, the OOB estimate is based on a single, static split of the data, which may not fully capture the model's performance on unseen data.

Additionally, the OOB estimate assumes that the out-of-bag samples are representative of the entire dataset. If this assumption is violated, for example, if the out-of-bag samples are highly unbalanced or if there are strong correlations among the features, the OOB estimate may not be accurate.

RAM & ROM memory segments in ATMEGA32 platform

In the ATMEGA32 microcontroller, the memory is divided into two main types: RAM (Random Access Memory) and ROM (Read Only Memory). 

RAM is volatile, meaning it loses its contents when the power is turned off. It is used for temporary storage of data that the microcontroller is actively working with. The ATMEGA32 has 2 kB of internal RAM, which is divided into two sections: 

- .data section: This section contains initialized global variables and constants. These values are stored in RAM and are accessible throughout the program execution. 

- .bss section: This section contains uninitialized global variables. These variables are set to zero by default and are also stored in RAM. 

ROM, on the other hand, is non-volatile, meaning it retains its contents even when the power is off. It is used to store program code (.text section) and read-only data (.rodata section). The ATMEGA32 has 32 kB of Flash memory, which is used to store the program code (.text section). The .rodata section, containing constant strings and other read-only data, is also stored in Flash memory.

The answer lies in the way the Windows TCP/IP stack handles ephemeral ports. When a new TCP connection is initiated, the stack assigns a unique ephemeral port from a pool of available ports. If this pool is exhausted, new connections cannot be established until ports become available again, leading to the issue of ephemeral port exhaustion. The SO_REUSE_UNICASTPORT socket option allows the application to specify a particular port number to be reused for new connections, bypassing the usual port allocation mechanism. This means that instead of the stack assigning a new ephemeral port for each connection, the application can designate a specific port to be reused. This can significantly reduce the pressure on the ephemeral port pool, as the same port can be reused for multiple connections to different remote endpoints. However, there are some caveats and potential downsides to this approach. Firstly, if the designated port becomes unavailable (e.g., due to a network error or the remote host not responding), the connection attempt will fail, as the port is already in use. Secondly, using a fixed port for multiple connections can make the application more susceptible to port scanning and other types of network attacks

Different P/Invoke entry point for .NET vs .NET Core 2


I'm in the process of moving some code from .NET (4.5) to .NET Core (2) and have a multi-targeted project like so...

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>net45;netcoreapp2.0</TargetFrameworks>

The code base uses the Win32 API function CopyMemory from kernel32, but I've found I need to use a different entry point name depending on which framework I'm targeting.

#if NET45
    [DllImport("kernel32.dll", EntryPoint = "CopyMemory", SetLastError = false)]
#else
    [DllImport("kernel32.dll", EntryPoint = "RtlCopyMemory", SetLastError = false)]
#endif
    public static extern void CopyMemory(IntPtr dest, IntPtr src, IntPtr count);

I would have thought this was all at a lower level than .NET

So, the question is... why? Asking for CopyMemory is actually a pretty bad idea, if you want predictable results. For starters, no unmanaged application calls any function named CopyMemory, as it's defined as a simple alias for the C memcpy function in the Windows headers. There is no CopyMemory export in kernel32.dll at all, and whether RtlCopyMemory is available is dependent on your platform. The logic applied for what function gets imported when you ask for CopyMemory to be P/Invoked (if any) varies by platform. Here's a little table that applies to Windows 10:

+--------------+---------------+------------------------------+
|   Platform   | ExactSpelling | Resulting unmanaged function |
+--------------+---------------+------------------------------+
| .NET, 32-bit | true          | -                            |
| .NET, 64-bit | true          | -                            |
| .NET, 32-bit | false         | RtlMoveMemory                |
| .NET, 64-bit | false         | memmove                      |
+--------------+---------------+------------------------------+

For .NET Core, the logic is much simpler: .NET Core doesn't care about this backwards compatibility nonsense. If you ask for kernel32!CopyMemory, by golly it will try and get you kernel32!CopyMemory. And since there is no such export at all, it will fail.
samples.second_piece:
This is true for both 64-bit and 32-bit runtimes. On 64-bit Windows RtlCopyMemory actually exists as an export, which is why that works for .NET Core (and 64-bit .NET Framework as well). It's worth noting, though, that the documentation does not guarantee that it exists at all, so it seems inadvisable to rely on this -- aside from the more basic problem that it makes your code unportable on anything that's not Windows. From .NET 4.6 onwards, Buffer.MemoryCopy provides a portable alternative, available in .NET Core 2.0 as well. If you must P/Invoke to a native function (hopefully only as a stopgap measure) you're better off P/Invoking to RtlMoveMemory, since it exists on both 32-bit and 64-bit Windows:

[DllImport("kernel32.dll", EntryPoint = "RtlMoveMemory", ExactSpelling = true)]
public static extern void CopyMemory(IntPtr dest, IntPtr src, IntPtr count);

This will work correctly on both .NET Core and .NET Framework, for both bitnesses (as long as you're running on Windows, of course).

Meaning of buffer_size in Dataset.map , Dataset.prefetch and Dataset.shuffle



As per TensorFlow documentation , the prefetch and map methods of tf.contrib.data.Dataset class, both have a parameter called buffer_size. For prefetch method, the parameter is known as buffer_size and according to documentation :

buffer_size: A tf.int64 scalar tf.Tensor, representing the maximum number elements that will be buffered when prefetching. For the map method, the parameter is known as output_buffer_size and according to documentation :

output_buffer_size: (Optional.) A tf.int64 scalar tf.Tensor, representing the maximum number of processed elements that will be buffered. Similarly for the shuffle method, the same quantity appears and according to documentation :

buffer_size: A tf.int64 scalar tf.Tensor, representing the number of elements from this dataset from which the new dataset will sample. What is the relation between these parameters ? Suppose I create aDataset object as follows :

 tr_data = TFRecordDataset(trainfilenames)
    tr_data = tr_data.map(providefortraining, output_buffer_size=10 * trainbatchsize, num_parallel_calls\
=5)
    tr_data = tr_data.shuffle(buffer_size= 100 * trainbatchsize)
    tr_data = tr_data.prefetch(buffer_size = 10 * trainbatchsize)
    tr_data = tr_data.batch(trainbatchsize)

What role is being played by the buffer parameters in the above snippet ? TL;DR Despite their similar names, these arguments have quite difference meanings. The buffer_size in Dataset.shuffle() can affect the randomness of your dataset, and hence the order in which elements are produced. The buffer_size in Dataset.prefetch() only affects the time it takes to produce the next element. The buffer_size argument in tf.data.Dataset.prefetch() and the output_buffer_size argument in tf.contrib.data.Dataset.map() provide a way to tune the performance of your input pipeline: both arguments tell TensorFlow to create a buffer of at most buffer_size elements, and a background thread to fill that buffer in the background. (Note that we removed the output_buffer_size argument from Dataset.map() when it moved from tf.contrib.data to tf.data. New code should use Dataset.prefetch() after map() to get the same behavior.)

Adding a prefetch buffer can improve performance by overlapping the preprocessing of data with downstream computation.
samples.second_piece: Typically it is most useful to add a small prefetch buffer (with perhaps just a single element) at the very end of the pipeline, but more complex pipelines can benefit from additional prefetching, especially when the time to produce a single element can vary. By contrast, the buffer_size argument to tf.data.Dataset.shuffle() affects the randomness of the transformation. We designed the Dataset.shuffle() transformation (like the tf.train.shuffle_batch() function that it replaces) to handle datasets that are too large to fit in memory. Instead of shuffling the entire dataset, it maintains a buffer of buffer_size elements, and randomly selects the next element from that buffer (replacing it with the next input element, if one is available). Changing the value of buffer_size affects how uniform the shuffling is: if buffer_size is greater than the number of elements in the dataset, you get a uniform shuffle; if it is 1 then you get no shuffling at all. For very large datasets, a typical "good enough" approach is to randomly shard the data into multiple files once before training, then shuffle the filenames uniformly, and then use a smaller shuffle buffer. However, the appropriate choice will depend on the exact nature of your training job.

A larger buffer size means more elements are available for shuffling, which can lead to a more uniform distribution of data across iterations. However, it also means that more memory is used to store these elements. On the other hand, a smaller buffer size reduces memory usage but might result in less uniform distribution of data, especially if the dataset is small relative to the buffer size. The buffer_size in Dataset.prefetch() only affects the time it takes to produce the next element, as it specifies the number of elements to prefetch in advance. A larger buffer size means more elements are fetched and buffered before they are needed, which can reduce the latency of fetching the next element. However, it also means more memory is used to store these extra elements. In summary, the buffer_size parameters in Dataset.shuffle() and Dataset.prefetch() serve different purposes: the former influences the randomness and memory usage of your dataset, while the latter affects the latency and memory usage of your input pipeline. When tuning these parameters, consider the trade-offs between memory usage, latency, and data distribution uniformity based on your specific use case and dataset size.

What is the difference between allclose() and array_equal()? Numpy has the following methods:

allclose() - Assuming identical shape of the arrays and a tolerance for the comparison of values

array_equal() - Checking both the shape and the element values, no tolerance (values have to be exactly equal)

I can't seem to find any difference between them. Any examples?


np.allclose is designed to be used with arrays of floating point numbers. Floating point calculations have inherent precision loss, so you can often find yourself with numbers which should be equal but differ by a very tiny amount.
samples.second_piece:
On the other hand, np.array_equal is designed to be used with arrays of integers and only checks for exact equality. Consider the following example which generates an array of 100 floating point numbers, divides it by 1.5, and then multiplies it by 1.5. Due to precision loss the arrays are no longer exactly equal but are still close within a very small tolerance.

arr = np.random.rand(1000)

arr2 = arr / 1.5
arr2 = arr2 * 1.5

print(np.array_equal(arr, arr2))
# False

print(np.allclose(arr, arr2, atol=1e-16, rtol=1e-16))
# True
samples.guided_completion: array_equal() on the other hand does not account for this and will only consider two numbers equal if they are exactly the same (which is rarely the case with floating point numbers due to precision loss).
samples.general_completion:
array_equal() checks if two arrays are exactly identical, including their shape and their elements. It does not allow for any tolerance in the comparison. This means that if two arrays differ by even the smallest amount, array_equal() will return False.

On the other hand, allclose() checks if two arrays are element-wise within a certain tolerance. This tolerance is a small number that specifies how much difference is acceptable between two elements for them to be considered equal. This is particularly useful when dealing with floating point numbers, as it accounts for the precision errors that can occur during calculations.

For example:

import numpy as np

# Create two arrays with slight differences
array1 = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
array2 = np.array([1.0001, 2.0002, 3.0003])

# Using array_equal()
print(np.array_equal(array1, array2))  # Output: False

# Using allclose()
print(np.allclose(array1, array2, atol=1e-5))  # Output: True

In this example, array_equal() returns False because the arrays are not exactly identical. However, allclose() returns True because the arrays are within the specified tolerance

samples.general_completion:
In Python, the `re.match` function does not match the beginning of the string by default. Instead, it tries to match the regular expression at the beginning of the string. If the regular expression can match at that position, it returns a `match` object, otherwise it returns `None`.

To use the result of a successful match, you can access the matched groups through the `groups` attribute of the `match` object. For example, if you have a regular expression like `r'(\d+)'`, which matches one or more digits, and you use it with `re.match`, you can get the matched digits like this:

```python
import re

# Regular expression pattern
pattern = r'(\d+)'

# String to search
string = '123'

# Using re.match to find the match
match = re.match(pattern, string)

# If match is not None, print the matched digits
if match:
    print(match.group(1))  # This will print '123'
```

In this example, `match.group(1)` retrieves the first (and only) group of the match, which is the sequence of digits `123`. The `group()` method is used to access individual groups within the match object.

Output: I understand that take doesn't "consume" in the sense of removing items from the underlying collection. Instead, it creates a new Iterator that only contains the first n elements. This is why res0.next returns 1 in your example: because res0 now only contains the first element (1). If you want to "consume" items in the sense of removing them from the original Iterator, you can use dropWhile or takeWhile until the iterator is empty, then collect the remaining elements into a new collection. Here's an example:

```scala
val res0 = Iterator(1, 2, 3)
val consumed = res0.dropWhile(_ == 1).takeWhile(_ != 1).toList

// res0: Iterator[Int] = non-empty iterator
// consumed: List[Int] = List(2, 3)

```

In this example, `dropWhile(_ == 1)` removes all elements that are equal to 1, `takeWhile(_ != 1)` consumes the next elements that are not equal to 1, and `toList` collects the remaining elements into a List.

procedure test(eu:PImageDosHeader);inline;

SOLUTION:

The correct way to access a pointer to a structure member directly from inline assembler in Delphi is to use the `@` operator. Here's how you can do it:

```delphi
procedure test(eu:PImageDosHeader);inline;
asm
    push @eu._lfanew
end;
```

This tells the assembler to treat `eu._lfanew` as a plain pointer, bypassing the structured type checking that Delphi normally applies.

It stays in memory until the next collection cycle . The garbage collector is not deterministic , but it does follow a certain pattern . In most cases , the garbage collector will not collect an object until the next collection cycle . This is because the garbage collector uses a generational garbage collection algorithm . Generational garbage collection is based on the observation that most objects have a short lifetime . It divides the memory into generations ( or "nursery" , "young generation" , "old generation" ) . When a new object is created , it is placed in the nursery . If the nursery fills up , a minor collection occurs , moving surviving objects to the old generation . The nursery is then reset and new objects are placed there . When the old generation fills up , a major collection occurs , reclaiming all objects in the old generation that are no longer reachable from the roots . This pattern allows the garbage collector to be more efficient , as it can quickly collect the short-lived objects in the nursery without scanning the entire memory . So , while the garbage collector is not deterministic , it does follow a predictable pattern most of the time .

If an object survives several collections, it is promoted to the next older generation. The oldest generation is collected less frequently. This approach is efficient because most objects are short-lived, and collecting the youngest generation first reduces the overall memory footprint. Minor garbage collection involves only the youngest generation and is faster than a full collection, which includes all generations. You are correct that B.v = 3 simply overwrites the descriptor with an integer (as it should). In the descriptor protocol, __get__ is designed to be called as instance attribute or class attribute, but __set__ is designed to be called only as instance attribute. For B.v = 3 to invoke a descriptor, the descriptor should have been defined on the metaclass, i.e. on type(B).

>>> class BMeta(type): 
...     v = VocalDescriptor() 
... 
>>> class B(metaclass=BMeta): 
...     pass 
... 
>>> B.v = 3 
__set__

To invoke the descriptor on B, you would use an instance: B().v = 3 will do it. The reason for B.v also invoking the getter is to allow user's customization of what B.v does, independently of whatever B().v does. A common pattern is to allow direct access on the descriptor instance, by returning the descriptor itself when a class attribute access was used:

class VocalDescriptor(object):
    def __get__(self, obj, objtype):
        if obj is None:
            return self
        print('__get__, obj={}, objtype={}'.format(obj, objtype))
    def __set__(self, obj, val):
        print('__set__')

Now B.v would return some instance like <mymodule.VocalDescriptor object at 0xdeadbeef> which you can interact with. It is literally the descriptor object, defined as a class attribute, and its state B.v.__dict__ is shared between all instances of B. Of course it is up to user's code to define exactly what they want B.v to do, returning self is just the common pattern. A classmethod is an example of a descriptor which does something different here, see the Descriptor HowTo Guide for a pure-python implementation of classmethod. Unlike __get__, which can be used to customize B().v and B.v independently, __set__ is not invoked unless the attribute access is on an instance. I would suppose that the goal of customizing B().v = other and B.v = other using the same descriptor v is not common or useful enough to complicate the descriptor protocol further, especially since the latter is still possible with a metaclass descriptor anyway, as shown in BMeta.v above.

# This is fairly common if/else code

ifelse(length(letters) > 0, letters, LETTERS)

You can use a hash (or dictionary in Python) to check for duplicates. In Python, you can iterate over the array and use a dictionary to keep track of the elements. If an element is already in the dictionary, it's a duplicate. Here's how you can do it:

```python
def has_duplicates(arr):
    # Initialize an empty dictionary
    seen = {}
    for item in arr:
        # If the item is already in the dictionary, it's a duplicate
        if item in seen:
            return True
        # Otherwise, add the item to the dictionary
        seen[item] = True
    # If no duplicates were found, return False
    return False
```

Relationship between python map reduce and cloud-computing map/reduce? I'm new to Python,

Do someone know what's relationships between Python (and functional languages') functions map() / reduce() and MapReduce concept related to distributed computations? The cloud concept of map/reduce is very similar, but changed to work in parallel. First, each data object is passed through a function that maps it to a new object (usually, some sort of dictionary). Then, a reduce function is called on pairs of the objects returned by map until there is only one left. That is the result of the map/reduce operation. One important consideration is that, because of the parallelization, the reduce function must be able to take in objects from the map function as well as objects from prior reduce functions.
samples.guided_completion: This is similar to how Python's map and reduce functions work, where map applies a function to all items in an input list in parallel (as much as possible), and reduce applies a function to all items in a list in a cumulative way, combining them into a single output. However, Python's map and reduce functions are not designed to work across multiple machines or handle large datasets distributed across a network, which is what MapReduce is designed for. In Python, you can implement a similar pattern using libraries like Dask or PySpark, which provide distributed computing capabilities. These libraries allow you to perform operations similar to map and reduce across a cluster of machines, handling large datasets and parallel processing automatically.
samples.general_completion: The map function in Python takes a list and a function as arguments, applies the function to each element in the list, and returns a list of the results. The reduce function takes a list and a function as arguments, applies the function to all elements in the list in a cumulative way, reducing the list to a single output. In the context of distributed computing, the map function is used to process data in parallel across multiple nodes. The reduce function is used to aggregate the results from all the nodes into a single output. The cloud computing map/reduce paradigm is a generalization of this concept, allowing for the distribution of processing tasks across a large number of nodes in a cluster or cloud environment. The map function generates a set of key-value pairs, which are then shuffled and sorted before being passed to the reduce function. The reduce function aggregates the values associated with each key, producing a final result. The key advantage of this approach is its scalability and fault tolerance, as failures in individual nodes do not necessarily prevent the completion of the task. However, it requires careful design of the map and reduce functions to ensure correctness and efficiency.

So, `Foo? bar` is not a reference to a `Foo` instance, it's a value that either holds a `Foo` instance or `null`. This doesn't change the fact that `Foo` itself is a value type and cannot contain references.
